newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: More lawsuits by small investors seen in S.Korea.
newsitem.headline: More lawsuits by small investors seen in S.Korea.

text.p: South Korea's first-ever shareholder lawsuit has signalled that the country's long-suffering small investors may finally be waking up to their rights, analysts said on Wednesday.

Aided by a civic organisation, a group of minority shareholders representing a 0.5 percent stake of Korea First Bank on Tuesday filed a lawsuit against four former bank executives in connection with loans to failed Hanbo Steel Co.
The shareholders said in their suit they were not seeking money for themselves but were demanding the four executives pay a 10 billion won indemnity to the bank over the loans extended to Hanbo.

"We just want bank management, who ignored minority shareholders and domineered the business operation, to accept their responsibilities," said Lee Seung-hee, a coordinator of the People's Solidarity for Participatory Democracy.

The suit alleged former bank presidents Sheen Kwang-shik and Rhee Chul-soo and two other executives were responsible for the bank's non-performing loans of 1.07 trillion won ($1.2 billion) to the steelmaker.

"It's not quite right to say bank presidents should assume all responsibilities for bank loans," a bank spokesman said. "It has not yet been determined if the loans to Hanbo actually constituted the bank's bad loans."
"If a third party takes over Hanbo, we will have no big problems with the loans," the spokesman added.
Korea First Bank is Hanbo's prime creditor. Hanbo collapsed in January after piling up more than five trillion won ($5.6 billion) in debts.
"I have not seen a previous occasion where small investors filed a suit for damages against a company," said Henry Morris, managing director of Coryo International (H.K.).
"It's just interesting to see people protesting not by going to the bank offices and carrying signs in a street campaign," he said.
A common and accepted form of showing dissatisfaction with anything from government to employers in South Korean has been to take to the streets.

Analysts said a revision to securities regulations in April made the lawsuit possible. The new regulations lowered the threshold for collective action by minority shareholders to 0.5 percent from the previous five percent.
"It will be the start of a trend," said one lawyer. "With help from civic groups, minority shareholders will be encouraged to realise and exercise their rights more often."
He said small investors were discouraged by high costs and complicated procedures from filing on their own.

Korea First Bank's shareholders had a good chance of winning their suit as the two former presidents have been jailed for four years and five years respectively for accepting bribes from Hanbo, he said.
Analysts said minority shareholders in Korea First Bank were angered by the bank's involvement in the loans-for-kickback scandal and subsequent losses.

"By buying bank shares, investors may not expect to get rich, but they probably expect banks to become reasonably profitable so that they can be paid dividends. They are quite disappointed and upset," Morris said.
The shareholders alleged the four executives played a leading role in the bank's decision to extend the loans without proper credit analysis.

Lee Keunmo, head of research at ING Barings said: "In Korea, small investors had been speculators for quick profits. But they now have turned into investors and have begun to realise their ownership rights and exercise them."
"So the number of lawyers will increase," he said.
Lee Young-man, senior economist at LG Economic Research Institute, said the collective action was "desirable" as the case would serve as a warning shot to lax management that "We are watching you".
"Management will perhaps have to be much more careful about the type of business they conduct in the future and try to ensure the company do not suffer extreme losses," Morris said.
Korea First Bank's share price has ranged from a 1997 high of 5,150 won to a low of 2,670. It closed on Wednesday at 4,150 won. ($1 = 891 won)
